note: Hand-written Science starter items anchored to NGSS (docs/03 §5): SC.PRAC.1 (priority 1: tables/graphs, variables, fair tests, conclusions) and the October physical-science skills. Distractors are documented misconceptions.

items.stem: A table shows how far a toy car rolled from a ramp: 10 cm ramp height → 40 cm; 20 cm → 80 cm; 30 cm → 120 cm. What happens to the distance as the ramp gets higher?
options: It cannot be told from the table.

distractor_rationale.D: the table shows a clear pattern

items.explanation: Each 10 cm of height adds about 40 cm of distance.
items.rule: SEP — read a data table and describe a pattern.

items.stem: In an experiment to see whether plants grow taller with more water, what is the thing being CHANGED on purpose (the independent variable)?
items.explanation: The scientist changes the water and measures the height.

items.stem: A bar graph shows rainfall in Baku: March 30 mm, April 25 mm, May 20 mm, June 8 mm. Which month was driest?
items.explanation: June has the smallest bar, 8 mm.

items.stem: Which question can be answered by a fair test?
options: Which brand of paper towel absorbs the most water?
items.explanation: A fair test needs something measurable.

items.stem: Elchin wants to test whether sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water. Which plan is a FAIR test?
options: Use the same amount of sugar and water, stir the same way, change only the water temperature.
Use more sugar in the hot water so it dissolves faster.
Stir the hot water but not the cold water.
Use a big cup for hot water and a small cup for cold.
items.explanation: In a fair test only one variable changes; everything else stays the same.

items.stem: A student measured how long ice took to melt: in the shade 45 minutes, in the sun 12 minutes, in a fridge 300 minutes. Which conclusion is supported by the data?
options: Ice melts faster where it is warmer.
Ice melts faster in the fridge.
Ice never melts in the shade.
items.explanation: The warmest place (sun) had the fastest melting.

items.stem: A table shows a plant's height each week: week 1 = 4 cm, week 2 = 7 cm, week 3 = 10 cm, week 4 = 13 cm. Describe the pattern and predict the height in week 5.
items.rubric: Must state the plant grows about 3 cm each week (steady growth) and predict about 16 cm for week 5. Accept 15–17 cm with the reasoning.
items.explanation: The height rises by 3 cm every week, so week 5 ≈ 16 cm.
items.rule: SEP — patterns and predictions from data.

items.stem: In the sugar experiment, what is the DEPENDENT variable (the thing you measure)?
options: The time it takes the sugar to dissolve
items.explanation: You measure how long dissolving takes.

items.stem: Two groups tested the same paper towel. Group A dipped it once and got 20 ml absorbed. Group B repeated the test five times and got 18, 21, 19, 20, 22 ml. Whose result is more reliable, and why?
options: Group B, because repeating the test shows the result is consistent.
Group A, because one test is quicker.
Group A, because 20 is a round number.
Neither, because the numbers are different.
items.explanation: Repeated trials reveal whether a result is consistent.

items.stem: A student concludes: "Plants near the window grew taller, so windows make plants grow." Explain what is wrong with this conclusion and what the real cause might be.
items.rubric: Must point out that the window itself is not the cause; the likely cause is more light (or warmth) near the window, and the test should compare light amounts with other conditions kept the same. Credit for naming a confounding factor.
items.explanation: The window is linked to more light; the light is the likely cause.
items.rule: SEP — cause vs correlation in conclusions.

items.stem: A line graph shows temperature during a day: 6 am 12°C, 9 am 16°C, 12 pm 23°C, 3 pm 26°C, 6 pm 21°C, 9 pm 15°C. When was it warmest, and what happened after that?
options: Warmest at 3 pm; then it cooled steadily.
Warmest at 12 pm; then it warmed further.
Warmest at 9 pm; then it cooled.
Warmest at 6 am; then it cooled.
items.explanation: 26°C at 3 pm is the peak; the values fall afterwards.

items.stem: Design a fair test to find out whether a ball bounces higher on concrete or on grass. List: what you will change, what you will keep the same (at least three things), and what you will measure.
items.rubric: Change: the surface only. Keep the same: the ball, the drop height, the way it is dropped/released, the measurer/method, the number of trials. Measure: bounce height (with a ruler/marks), repeated several times. All three parts needed for full credit.
items.explanation: One variable changes; the rest stay constant; the outcome is measured the same way each time.

items.stem: When sugar dissolves in water and disappears from sight, what has happened to it?
options: It has broken into particles too small to see, spread through the water.
It has floated away into the air.

distractor_rationale.D: it is still in the water — taste it

items.explanation: The sugar particles are still there, mixed among the water particles.
items.rule: 5-PS1-1 — matter is made of particles too small to see.

items.stem: Which is evidence that air is made of matter, even though you cannot see it?
options: A balloon gets bigger when you blow into it.
You cannot hold air in your hand.
items.explanation: Something must be filling the balloon and pushing its sides out.

items.stem: A wet towel dries on the line. Where does the water go?
options: It evaporates into the air as invisible water vapour.
items.explanation: The water particles leave the towel and spread into the air.

items.stem: You smell bread baking from another room. What does this show about the particles from the bread?
options: They travel through the air and reach your nose.
The smell is not made of anything.
The bread is in your nose.
items.explanation: Tiny particles from the bread spread through the air.

items.stem: Explain why a sealed, empty-looking plastic bottle cannot be squashed flat easily.
items.rubric: Must say the bottle is full of air, which is made of particles that take up space and push back when squeezed. Credit for 'air is matter/has particles/takes up space'.
items.explanation: The air inside is matter; its particles push back.

items.stem: Which model best shows why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller space but a solid cannot?
options: Gas particles are far apart with empty space between them; solid particles are packed tightly.
Gas particles are larger than solid particles.
Gas is not made of particles.
items.explanation: Squeezing a gas pushes its widely spaced particles closer.

items.stem: A student says: "When the puddle dried up, the water was gone for good." Use the particle model to explain why this is wrong, and describe one observation that supports your explanation.
items.rubric: Must explain that the water became water vapour (particles spread into the air) and still exists; a supporting observation such as condensation on a cold glass/mirror, or clouds/rain, or humidity. Both parts needed.
items.explanation: Evaporated water is still matter; it condenses back on cold surfaces.
items.rule: 5-PS1-1 — explain with a particle model and evidence.

items.stem: A balloon filled with air is put in a freezer and shrinks. Which explanation fits the particle model?
options: The cold air particles move more slowly and take up less space, so the balloon shrinks.
The balloon's rubber ate the air.
items.explanation: Slower particles push out less, so the balloon takes up less space.

items.stem: Which observation is the BEST evidence that dissolved salt is still present in water?
options: The water tastes salty and, when it evaporates, salt crystals remain.
The salt made a sound when it was poured.

distractor_rationale.B: looking clear does not prove it is gone or present

items.explanation: Taste and the crystals left after evaporation show the salt never left.

items.stem: Which property would help you tell iron from aluminium?
options: Whether a magnet sticks to it

distractor_rationale.C: shape is not a property of the material

items.explanation: Iron is magnetic; aluminium is not.

items.stem: Which of these is a property of a material?

distractor_rationale.B: not a property of the material

items.explanation: Solubility is a property of the substance itself.

items.stem: A wire must carry electricity to a lamp. Which property matters most when choosing its material?
items.explanation: Metals like copper conduct electricity well.

items.stem: You have two white powders: salt and chalk dust. Describe a test using water that would tell them apart, and what you would see.
items.rubric: Stir each into water: salt dissolves (solution becomes clear), chalk does not (cloudy, settles at the bottom). Must name solubility/dissolving and the observation.
items.explanation: Salt is soluble; chalk is not.

items.stem: Which pair of properties would BEST identify a small piece of unknown material?
options: Whether it dissolves in water and whether a magnet attracts it
Its size and its position on the table
How far away it is and how heavy the table is
items.explanation: Solubility and magnetism depend on the material, not the sample.

items.stem: A table gives properties of three unknown solids: A — dissolves, not magnetic, conducts no electricity; B — does not dissolve, magnetic, conducts electricity; C — does not dissolve, not magnetic, conducts electricity. Which is most likely iron, which is salt, and which is copper? Explain using the table.
items.rubric: B = iron (magnetic, conducts), A = salt (dissolves, no conduction), C = copper (conducts, not magnetic, insoluble). Must justify with at least two properties.
items.explanation: Iron is magnetic; copper conducts but is not magnetic; salt dissolves.
items.rule: 5-PS1-3 — identify materials from a property table.

items.stem: Why is 'it is heavy' a poor way to identify a material?
options: Because heaviness depends on how big the piece is, not only on the material.
Because heavy things are always iron.
items.explanation: A big piece of wood can be heavier than a tiny piece of iron; density, not weight, is the property.

items.stem: Ice cubes with a mass of 50 g melt completely in a sealed bag. What is the mass of the water?
items.explanation: Melting changes the state, not the amount of matter.

items.stem: 10 g of salt is stirred into 100 g of water until it disappears. What is the total mass now?
options: 110 g, because the salt is still there, dissolved
items.explanation: Dissolving does not destroy the salt; 100 + 10 = 110 g.

items.stem: A student weighs a candle (30 g), burns it for ten minutes, and finds it now weighs 22 g. She says mass was destroyed. Explain what really happened to the missing 8 g.
items.rubric: Must explain the wax turned into gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour) and smoke that went into the air; if everything were collected in a sealed container the total mass would still be 30 g. Credit for 'gases escaped'.
items.explanation: The wax became gases that escaped; mass was conserved overall.
items.rule: 5-PS1-2 — conservation of mass in an open system.
